system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-08-05 01:42:00 to 2134-08-16 13:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of chronic left shoulder pain due to rotator cuff tears, SIADH, and aortic stenosis was admitted for severe worsening shoulder pain and a low sodium level of 118. Evaluation revealed septic arthritis of the left shoulder caused by Streptococcus viridans, confirmed by joint fluid analysis. He underwent open irrigation and debridement and was started on intravenous vancomycin, with a PICC line placed for long-term antibiotic therapy. During the hospitalization, he developed transient atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which resolved spontaneously; he was started on warfarin with a heparin bridge for stroke prevention. His hyponatremia, attributed to SIADH exacerbated by pain, improved with fluid restriction. He remained afebrile with decreasing white blood cell count and was discharged to extended care for completion of a four-week antibiotic course, ongoing anticoagulation management, and rehabilitation.

INDICATION:  ___ man with cellulitis and shoulder pain.

with history of previous left septic joint, status post wash-out in early
___.

radiographs from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial CT images were acquired through the left shoulder in the
absence of intravenous contrast.  Note the contrast was not administered per
patient request.  Coronal and sagittal reformatted images were also reviewed.

FINDINGS:  Hypodensity is visualized surrounding the left shoulder joint
consistent with an effusion.  Hypodensity is also visualized superior to the
humeral head, likely representing fluid in the subacromial and subdeltoid
bursa.  Enhancement characteristics of the wall of this effusion are not
assessed in the absence of intravenous contrast.  Bony erosions are visualized
in the acromion, clavicular head, humeral head and to a lesser degree in the
glenoid.  These findings appear new or progressed since ___, though are
similar to those seen on comparison radiograph and raise concern for
infectious related osteolysis.  The imaged portions of the left hemithorax are
notable for a left pleural effusion.  The portions of the heart reveal
extensive coronary arterial calcification.  A central line terminates at the
superior cavoatrial junction.  The remainder of the visualized skeleton is
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  Left glenohumeral joint effusion as above.  Given the recent
history and current clinical presentation, this raises concern for possible
septic arthritis.  Also noted are underlying osseous erosive changes,
progressed from ___, but appearing similar to that seen recently, possibly
representing osteolysis related to septic arthritis.

AP CHEST 01:00 A.M. ON ___

HISTORY:  A ___ man with a PIC placement.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

The right PIC line ends in the region of the superior cavoatrial junction. 
Bilateral pleural effusion, small on the left, tiny on the right has
increased.  Borderline cardiomegaly is stable.  Mediastinal vasculature
borderline enlarged, no pulmonary edema.  Fullness in the upper mediastinum
probably due to tortuous head and neck vessels.

FLUOROSCOPIC-GUIDED ASPIRATION OF BILATERAL SHOULDER JOINTS

INDICATION:  History of strep viridans arthritis of left shoulder now
bacteremic, concern for recurrence of septic arthritis at left shoulder and
new right shoulder septic arthritis.

TECHNIQUE:  Written informed consent from the patient's next of kin was
obtained over the telephone by Dr. ___ Dr. ___.  The
procedure was performed with the assistance of an interpreter.  A preprocedure
timeout confirming patient identity, procedure side and site was performed.

A suitable position for aspiration of the right shoulder was marked in the
skin with fluoroscopic assistance.  The skin was prepped with Betadine.  1%
lidocaine was used to anesthetize the skin and subcutaneous tissues.  Under
intermittent fluoroscopic guidance, a 20-gauge spinal needle was advanced into
the right glenohumeral joint.  Approximately 6 cc of cloudy fluid was
aspirated.  This sample was sent for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity in
addition to cell count and differential.

A separate procedure was then performed to aspirate the left shoulder.  The
left shoulder was prepped with Betadine.  Under intermittent fluoroscopic
guidance, a 20-gauge spinal needle was advanced into the left glenohumeral
joint.  Approximately 6 cc of blood-stained fluid was aspirated from the left
shoulder joint.  This was sent for cell count and differential in addition to
Gram stain, culture and sensitivity.  The procedure was well tolerated.  

___, the attending physician, was present and available throughout
the procedure.

IMAGING FINDINGS:
Fluoroscopic images of the right shoulder demonstrate complete obliteration of
the acromiohumeral interval compatible with a full-thickness rotator cuff
tear.  Degenerative changes are seen at the right humeral head.  Injection of
contrast into the left glenohumeral joint demonstrated extension of contrast
through the left acromioclavicular joint compatible with extension of contrast
through rotator cuff tear into the subacromial/subdeltoid space and through
the acromiohumeral interval.  This is compatible with a full-thickness rotator
cuff tear.  There is also a complete effacement of the acromiohumeral interval
on the left.  There is abnormal lucency at the articular surface of the left
humerus unchanged from prior examination on ___.

IMPRESSION:  
1. Successful aspiration of fluid from bilateral shoulder joints and sample
sent separately for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity in addition to cell
count and differential from each shoulder.
2. Bilateral narrowing of acromio-humeral interval compatible with full-
thickness rotator cuff tears.

Given presence for two to ___ years and lack of surrounding erythema and

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening, sir. I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in because of redness and swelling in your left shoulder. Can you tell me more about how it’s been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s red and warm, but not very painful. I had surgery on it before, and it was getting better at rehab. Now this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on vancomycin at rehab. We’ve started you on clindamycin tonight since you already got your dose. We’re concerned this might be an infection, so we’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected again? I don’t have fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not sure yet. Your temperature is normal, but we found bacteria in your blood — strep viridans. That’s the same bug from your last infection. So we need to check if it’s back in your joint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my shoulder might be infected again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. A CT scan shows fluid in the joint and some bone changes that could mean infection. But we won’t know for sure until we test the fluid. Orthopedics and infectious disease are reviewing your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my legs? They’re swollen and red too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your legs have a rash and swelling. The team thinks it’s lipodermatosclerosis — a skin condition from poor circulation. We’ll keep using the compression bandages and creams you had at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my constipation — I need my usual medicines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your bisacodyl and added docusate. You can also use lactulose if needed. We’ll make sure you keep your routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures confirmed strep viridans. We’re treating it with antibiotics. The PICC line you had was removed as a possible source, even though it looked okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the line could have caused this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we can’t be sure. Since you’re on long-term antibiotics, we’ll place a new PICC line later this week for the medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Orthopedics don’t think the left shoulder is infected again. But we’re worried about your right shoulder — you never had pain there, but the bacteria might have spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a procedure tomorrow to draw fluid from both shoulders. That will tell us if either joint is infected. It’s done with imaging guidance and local numbing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both? Even the one that doesn’t hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because sometimes infections don’t cause pain at first. Better to check both. The results will guide whether you need more treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the results from today’s joint taps. Your left shoulder looks clear — no white cells or bacteria. But your right shoulder had 15,000 white blood cells. That suggests early infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I don’t feel pain there. Is it really infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be. The culture didn’t grow bacteria, but the high cell count is concerning. We’re treating it as possible septic arthritis. We’ll repeat the tap in a few days to see if the count is going down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics? Still on clindamycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to ceftriaxone. The bacteria is sensitive to penicillin, but you’re allergic, so we can’t use that. Ceftriaxone is safe and effective. We’ll give it through a new PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound showed no blood clot in the arm. The redness is likely from the old IV site. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And that lump in my elbow? It’s been there years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows it’s likely a benign nodule, maybe a lipoma. It’s not infected. No need to treat it now unless it changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative — that’s good. The new antibiotics are working. Your sodium is a bit low, but we’re managing it with fluid restriction, as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time? I’ll be careful with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your heart is stable — you have aortic stenosis, but your echo shows good function. Your atrial fibrillation is controlled with metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m supposed to have a spinal injection soon. Do I stop my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve held your warfarin. You’ll restart it after the injection. We’re using heparin injections in the meantime to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tapped your right shoulder again today. The white blood cell count dropped to 1,200 — that’s a big improvement. It means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks like it was early infection. No bacteria grew, but the response to treatment confirms it. You’ll finish a full course of ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the redness on my left shoulder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dermatology saw you. It’s not cellulitis. It’s likely from surgery and will fade. No need for more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. ESR is coming down, which means less inflammation. We’re continuing ceftriaxone via PICC. You’ll need weekly blood tests to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to extended care. You’ll finish antibiotics there, and we’ll arrange follow-up with infectious disease and orthopedics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain patches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can keep using the lidocaine patches — two on the right, one on the left. You haven’t needed oxycodone, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows small pleural effusions, but they’re stable. No sign of heart failure. Your lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re breathing well. We’ll keep your albuterol nebs as needed. Your chronic bronchitis is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge tomorrow. You’ll go to extended care with the PICC line for ceftriaxone. Make sure they check your blood weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart it after your spinal injection. The rehab team will coordinate that with your pain doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my creams and bowel routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual creams and bowel meds are on your discharge list. You’re in charge of that — we’ll make sure the facility follows your preferences.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — your vitals are stable, labs are good. You’re ready to go tomorrow. Any questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long on the IV antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until your infectious disease visit. They’ll decide when to stop based on your progress and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the shoulder pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the lidocaine patches. See orthopedics in two weeks. The pain should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll leave in a few hours. All your meds are ready, and the facility has been contacted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take everything as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep all your follow-up appointments. Call if you develop fever, redness, or shortness of breath. Otherwise, we expect steady recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my son wants to know about the spinal injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: He can call the pain clinic. You’re scheduled for next week. Warfarin restarts after that. I’ll make sure they have the note.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. He’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll fax your records today. Safe travels to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. We’re here if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of septic arthritis of the left shoulder, aortic stenosis, and SIADH was admitted from rehab with erythema of the left shoulder and found to have strep viridans bacteremia. Though the left shoulder was not reinfected, fluid from the right shoulder showed elevated white blood cells, indicating early septic arthritis. He was treated with ceftriaxone after switching from clindamycin, and a new PICC line was placed for antibiotic administration. His shoulder erythema was determined to be non-infectious, likely post-surgical. Hyponatremia improved with fluid restriction, and warfarin was held ahead of a planned spinal injection. He remained stable, with improving inflammatory markers, and was discharged to extended care for completion of antibiotics, follow-up with infectious disease and orthopedics, and resumption of anticoagulation after the procedure.
